A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same CodeFlowBench study. Their main text, equations, tables, figures and appendices support reliable comparison, including matching material relocated between the main text and appendices.

before.justification: v3 reports original evaluations of 19 LLMs on CodeFlowBench-Comp and CodeFlowBench-Repo, error analysis, and pipeline and human evaluations in Tables 1–6.

after.justification: v4 reports the retained benchmark evaluations and additional original code-quality, chronological, stopping-policy and topological-order analyses in Tables 11–14.

M1.justification: The data-curation pipeline, function-dependency decomposition, solution generation, unit-test construction and primary codeflow procedure remain unchanged. The new teacher-forcing experiment is an evaluation ablation, not a replacement of the proposed method.

E1.justification: Both versions retain the same competitive-programming collection and five-domain repository coverage. The chronological slices and selected subsets used for new analyses concern retained tasks; they do not introduce another dataset, domain or programming task.

E2.justification: The 19 evaluated models and single-turn comparison in Tables 1–2 remain unchanged, as do the pipeline comparators in Tables 4–6. New analyses reuse existing models; the non-stop condition changes the evaluation protocol rather than introducing another model or generation baseline.

E3.justification: Appendix E adds substantial evaluation designs: static analysis of successful multi-step completions, chronological slices matched on difficulty and structure, a 100-problem teacher-forcing control with Absolute Solved Turns, and four valid orderings of 100 nonlinear problems. The existing main sampling procedure and prompts are retained; Table 9 newly discloses inference settings rather than establishing a change to them.

E4.justification: v4 adds four substantive analyses testing software-quality benefits, chronological contamination risk, the effect of stopping after failures, and sensitivity to dependency ordering (Appendix E.1–E.4; Tables 11–14). The earlier pipeline ablations, error cases and dependency-complexity analysis remain, with the latter relocated into the main text.

E5.justification: Beyond the retained sampling-distribution chi-square test, v4 introduces 1,000 bootstrap resamples and standard errors for selected models' main results (Appendix D.3, Table 10), describing their use for approximate 95% confidence intervals. Table 14 also reports APT means and standard deviations across four orderings. These additions do not establish additional generation seeds or repeated model runs.

E6.justification: Tables 1–8 and existing result plots retain their values, but Tables 11–14 add substantial findings. Table 13 reports Gemini-3 AST of 1.19 under fail-stop versus 1.35 under non-stop evaluation. Table 11 shows lower multi-turn complexity for Gemini-3 and Claude-4.5, but higher GPT-5 complexity (6.62 versus 5.29). These are new analysis-specific results, not performance gains between versions.

T1.justification: Appendix E.3 newly defines Absolute Solved Turns as the count of correctly solved subproblems when failed predecessors are replaced with reference implementations. The existing PD/APD estimators and derivation remain unchanged in substance; Equation 2 merely omits an equivalent intermediate expectation expansion. No new proof is added.

C1.justification: The abstract, three central contributions and conclusion retain the same claims about the benchmark, automated pipeline, structural metrics and multi-turn performance gap. The introduction clarifies iterative implementation versus refinement without changing the previously described constructive task.

C2.justification: v4 substantially expands interpretation: Section 3.1 asserts that decomposition enforces software-design principles, while Appendix E argues for maintainability benefits, resistance to memorization, capability-driven failures and ordering stability. These arguments were absent from v3. The explicit limitations remain unchanged, and some new causal and reliability conclusions exceed what the limited controls establish.

D1.justification: Table 9 newly documents temperature 0.6, top-p 1.0, frequency penalty 0.0, and token limits of 5,000 for API inference and 10,000 locally. Appendix E.1 identifies static-analysis tooling such as radon. Existing prompts, container information, curation-cost estimates and code/data access targets remain unchanged.

R1.justification: The reference list and Related Work section are unchanged. The positioning against single-turn, interactive-feedback and simpler multi-turn benchmarks, including the claimed novelty of codeflow benchmarking, is retained.

P1.justification: v4 refines the task explanation and pipeline remark, adds affiliations and acknowledgements, and reorganizes the appendices around the new analyses. Existing dataset-statistics and DSC discussion move into the main text. Most prose and the main section sequence remain intact.

P2.justification: The presentation substantially expands through Tables 9–14 for settings, uncertainty and validation results. The competitive-programming statistics and DSC heatmap move from v3 Figures 12 and 16 into v4 Figures 4 and 6, with changed sizing and panel arrangement. Existing illustrations and tables are redistributed around these additions; their underlying figure content is retained.

improvement.justification: Compared with v3, v4 improves reproducibility through explicit inference settings and makes benchmark validity easier to assess through uncertainty estimates and targeted controls. The gains are limited by reporting and interpretation weaknesses: Table 10 displays standard errors under a confidence-interval heading, and the selected-subset contamination and fail-stop analyses do not establish their strongest conclusions. The additions provide useful evidence without fully resolving these concerns.
